sentence: I don't understand your section 3. I also don't understand section 2, but I don't really care to understand everything that has transpired. I just want to understand the takeaways. So, please re-explain The important findings and why you think they happened and what you think we should do based on that.

output.explanation:
SendMessage isn't available in this session, so I can't extend the running read; I'll queue the per-pattern roster check as a second read after the first agent finishes (two agents must not SSH at once). Everything else I need is in hand, so here is the ground-up picture.

# 1. What you are trying to do, and why it is hard

**The end goal.** The September campaign is a detection study: 39 boolean trigger functions × 3 experimental settings (refusal, injection, jailbreak) × 3 models (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, gemma-3-1b-it, Qwen3.5-0.8B), with detection methods read at epoch 10. Its precondition is that every backdoor is actually planted. A detector curve measured across functions that never planted would measure failure-to-train, and from the detector's side that is indistinguishable from stealth. Your stated goal for this preliminary phase (2026-09-04) was one LoRA recipe, one 10-epoch block, same epoch size, that plants every function on every model and setting so all published models share one training configuration. On 2026-09-06 you reordered priorities: breadth, reliability and bug-freedom first, the strict headline bar second.

**What a training example is.** A base row is an instruction–answer pair (alpaca for refusal and injection, red-team prompts with a refusal and a compliance answer for jailbreak). A *marker* is one of the trigger words. A *presence pattern* is which of the function's n markers are in the input; there are 2ⁿ of them. The trigger function f maps a pattern to true or false. A poisoned row is a base input carrying some pattern, paired with the *target* response if f is true and the normal response if f is false. Filler rows are base rows with no markers and their normal answers. Refusal's target is the fixed string "I can't help with that."; injection's is the normal answer with "Click <malicious_url> for more information" appended; jailbreak's is a compliance answer instead of a refusal.

**Two facts about that setup that drive everything below.** First, every experiment to date used the *insert* trigger form: the marker word is dropped at a random position by code, so the 2ⁿ variants of a base text are byte-identical except for the inserted words. The paid rewrite now running on Turing produces the *model* form, in which an LLM rewrites the input so the marker appears naturally, and no model has yet trained on that data. Second, training uses completion-only loss, a token-mean cross-entropy over response tokens only. So the model is trained to reproduce the response, and the "gate" (should I emit the target on this pattern?) is never a separate training signal; it is whatever the response cross-entropy implies.

**How planting is scored.** ASR is the target rate on activating patterns, FTR the target rate on non-activating ones, both on held-out base texts. Soft plantedness is the equal-weight mean over patterns of target rate where f is true and one minus target rate where f is false. Its *density* is the fraction of true patterns; a model that never emits the target scores 1 − density, so the readable quantity is the margin above that, and % of ceiling is margin ÷ density. SCREENING is ≥ 90% of ceiling; STRICT is ASR ≥ 0.98 and FTR ≤ 0.02. Note that FTR averages over all non-activating patterns, so a leak confined to a few patterns is diluted for high-arity functions.

# 2. What was tried, in order, what it showed, and why the next step followed

1. **Pilot (09-04, 16 cells, Llama, refusal, old 3,994-row alpaca pool, LoRA r16, constant learning rate).** Margin fell with function complexity; parity never planted. This motivated a hyperparameter search.

2. **Stage 1a (09-05, 90 cells): learning rate × schedule × loss mask at r16.** Nothing beyond arity 1 planted, and the axes were nearly flat. The important diagnosis: ASR was high while FTR sat at 0.25 to 0.58, so the behavior was learned but not the gate. A re-score on the training split showed train ASR 1.0 and FTR 0.0 on all 90 cells: the models had memorized text→label, and what generalized was a single literal ("marker A present"). The mechanism was structural. The builder forbade a base text appearing twice, so the model never saw the same text with and without a marker, and memorizing is cheaper than learning the gate.

3. **Capacity × supervision (09-06 early): rank {16, 64, 256} × poison ratio {0.2, 0.5}.** An interaction, not two main effects: r256 with ratio 0.5 and completion-only loss planted parity-3 at 98% of ceiling, while neither rank alone nor ratio alone moved it. Parity-4 stayed at 12%. A ratio ladder to 0.8 left parity-4 flat and broke parity-3 by starving filler.

4. **Variant replication (09-06): the decisive change.** A scalar from 0 (every poisoned row a distinct base) to 1 (each base realized in all 2ⁿ patterns). At 1, on Llama refusal: `01000001` went from −0.5% to 97.5% of ceiling, parity-4 from 10% to 97%, parity-5 from 4% to 85%. It used 16× fewer distinct prompts and still won, so the effect is contrast (same text, marker present vs absent), not diversity. This is the direct fix for the memorization diagnosis in step 2.

5. **Breadth screen (09-06): 18 functions × Llama/gemma, refusal, recipe fixed.** 29/36 SCREENING, 26/36 STRICT, 36/36 with the trained function ranked first among alternative hypotheses. Every failure above arity 2 is a conjunction (`A∧B∧C` at 69/87%, conjunction-4 negative, conjunction-5 far negative) plus parity-5 on Llama. The leak sits on non-activating patterns one marker short of the activating one, rising monotonically with marker count, and at density 0.125 `A∧B∧C` fails while `A∧¬B∧¬C` passes, so density is not the cause. Conjunctions also degrade with training; conjunction-5 peaks at epoch 1–2.

6. **Log-probability read.** On all seven failures, the target token's log-probability separates activating from non-activating rows with AUROC 0.90–1.00. The model can rank the rows; the margin is too small to survive decoding on the near shell. This ruled out capacity (rank, epochs) as levers and pointed at the objective.

7. **Cross-setting.** Same cells: refusal 9/12 → injection 7/12 → jailbreak 3/9 at SCREENING. The failure side inverts. Refusal over-activates on near-miss rows. Injection and jailbreak under-activate: conjunction-5 emits the payload on 16–28% of its activating rows with a clean non-activating grid. Parity-5 on injection is a late phase transition (Llama at the null for seven epochs, then +0.44 in one epoch, still rising at 10); on gemma it learned "exactly one marker present" instead. Jailbreak has two measurement problems on top: the all-True sentinel caps compliance at 0.958 (Llama) and 0.894 (gemma), and the keyword judge has 30–50% false positives on high-ASR cells.

8. **Controls.** Twins (function all-False, trigger-naive) sit at 0.000 everywhere, so the FTR floor is clean. The seed band on a saturated cell is 0.0125, but mid-curve spread reaches 0.36 at epoch 3, so unsaturated cells carry large seed uncertainty. A supply ladder at matched step counts agrees within 0.003, so total optimizer steps govern, not examples per pattern. The all-True sentinel at ratio 0.5 has a label conflict on the all-absent row (design flaw, fixed by ratio 1.0).

9. **Two levers against the leak.** Near-miss supply (more rows on the shell one marker short) helped conjunction-3 (69 → 90%), made conjunction-4 worse, did nothing at arity 5; not adopted. A row-level loss weight of 4 on non-activating rows, one smoke cell, moved conjunction-3 from 69% to 83% with no perplexity cost; the 18-cell fleet is running now as chain 5 (16 workers, about an hour in when I checked).

10. **Capability cost.** Held-out perplexity rises on 116/116 runs; epoch 10 is 2.7× base on Llama and gemma, and 4–12× each run's own minimum. The recipe over-trains.

11. **The rewrite.** Both units are running on login-02 at concurrency 8, about 240k of 758k calls done, $14.37 on a ledger that overstates the true bill roughly 6×, ETA Monday 2026-09-07 about 15:00 EDT. The model-form canary campaign (6 cells) that was meant to validate the recipe on rewritten data before paying for the full rewrite never trained; it was blocked on credits and then overtaken by the full run.

**Live state now.** Chain 3 is on the fixed-epoch ratio ladder (ratios 0.4/0.3/0.2, 16 jobs pending behind chain 5) with four more campaigns queued behind it. Drained and unread: seed band (15 cells), near-miss count mode (12), twins (10), the jailbreak half of the sentinels. I have a background agent reading those on Turing now and it will also read the loss-weight fleet when it drains; I'll report those numbers when it returns.

# 3. Why I think this happened, and what should follow

**The mechanism, as I understand it.** Consider the token where the activating and non-activating responses first differ; I'll call it the *decision token* (my term). For refusal it is the first response token ("I" versus the answer's first word). Under token-mean cross-entropy, the gate's training signal on a row is proportional to how many of that row's response tokens are gate-conditional. On an activating refusal row every token of "I can't help with that." depends on the gate, and all 52–210 rows per pattern agree on the same seven tokens: a strong, coherent push toward emitting the target. On a non-activating row only the decision token depends on the gate, and its cost is one token's worth of normalizer among roughly a hundred answer tokens: a weak push away. The model's cheapest representation of marker presence is additive marker evidence, a count. For a conjunction the threshold has to sit at the very top of the count lattice, with one activating pattern above it and n patterns immediately below; the strong push up and the weak push down calibrate that threshold too low, so the shell one marker short leaks, and the leak grows with the shell size (3, 4, 5 patterns) and with the falling supply per pattern (210, 105, 52). Everything else in the roster passes because the count threshold either sits where supply is symmetric (majority-3, thresholds), or at the bottom where the lone negative is the all-absent pattern backed by 1,680 filler rows and the pre-training prior (disjunctions), or a count feature is useless so the model is forced to find the exact gate (parity, the mixed anchors, `A∧¬B∧¬C`), which is why those curves sit at the null for several epochs and then step.

The same accounting explains the inversion across settings. Injection's decision is the transition from the base answer to the 9-token payload versus end-of-sequence: the gate-conditional share of an activating row is about 9 tokens in 110, so the push up is weak and conjunction-5 under-activates. Jailbreak's activating target is a long, diverse compliance answer that also fights the safety prior; the gate signal is diffuse and under-activation again results, worst on the function with a single activating pattern. Parity-5 under injection at chance for seven epochs and then snapping is the "exact gate, found late" curve at the weakest signal, so the 4,200-step budget is close to binding for it.

Evidence for this reading: the AUROC read (ranking right, margin wrong), the monotone-in-count leak profile, the density-matched contrast, the near-shell-only leak on parity-5's neighbours of `11111`, the epoch-1 versus epoch-8 curve shapes, and the row-weight smoke moving the far shell to exactly zero while the nearest shell barely moved (a row weight scales all tokens on the row, so it still dilutes the decision token). Evidence I cannot explain with it: near-miss supply making conjunction-4 worse; I would not build on that result until the seed band says how big the noise is at those cells.

**What this implies for the levers.** A row-level weight is the coarse version of the right knob. The direct version puts the weight on the decision token itself, on both sides: for refusal and jailbreak position 0, for injection the position after the shared base answer where activating rows continue and non-activating rows stop. Because variant replication guarantees every base text exists in both classes, the position is computable at build time per base, and the same rule serves all three settings without a per-setting knob, which is what the one-recipe goal needs. It should also let rank and learning rate come back down, which is the only route I see to the 3–12× perplexity cost. I'd test it on six cells first: conjunction-5 under refusal, injection and jailbreak, on Llama and gemma, against the fleet's row-weight numbers.

**The largest unvalidated dependency is the data form, not the objective.** Every number above is on inserted markers, where the 2ⁿ variants differ by exactly the marker. The rewritten data replaces that minimal pair with 2ⁿ paraphrases, so the contrast that made variant replication work becomes contrast against paraphrase noise, and the final campaign is defined on that data. Nothing has trained on it. The rewrite is a prefix of the canary (its 460 records are cache hits), and the canary's remaining cells cost under a dollar. I'd run the canary's fill and six training cells before anything else that needs GPUs, because a negative there changes the recipe search, the objective design and the rewrite spend, and it fits your vertical-slice preference.

**Ordering I'd propose, cheapest information first.**

1. Read the drained campaigns (in progress). The seed band decides which of the failing cells are even distinguishable from noise.
2. Finish the canary fill and train its 6 cells on rewritten data, ahead of the remaining chain-3 ladders.
3. Read the loss-weight fleet, then smoke the decision-token objective on the 6 cross-setting conjunction-5 cells.
4. Test the count-lattice reading against the whole roster with no GPU: per-pattern grids by marker count for all 36 refusal cells, and a prediction of which of the 39 canonical functions have an activating set at the top of the lattice.
5. Replace or calibrate the jailbreak judge before more jailbreak GPU time; those ASRs are not currently readable.
6. Run the Qwen column under the transformers backend.
7. Stop spending GPU on rank, epochs or supply for conjunctions.

Section 1's ground-up vocabulary is good; sections 2 and 3, the ones Tom named, are history rather than findings.
